passage: At sixteen, Farhan's results came back worse than he had feared, and the same week his parents began arguing behind a closed door over the shop's bills. He sat on the roof with his marks on his knee. His aunt Lakshmi found him there and said, "This is a lot at once. Come down and eat, and tomorrow we look at what you can retake." He ate. The next week he wrote a list of the subjects he could try again and asked his teacher to explain his mistakes. Hope came back slowly. At twenty, in his second year of engineering, he failed a paper just as his father was admitted to hospital and the next fee date drew near. He stopped answering messages and slept badly. Instead of holding it all, he made himself go to the counsellor, Ramesh, and said it all out loud. Ramesh helped him list the three pressures and sent him to the scholarship office and the faculty adviser the same afternoon. Farhan went to his father's bedside that evening with a shorter list and slightly lighter shoulders.

qa.q: Who found Farhan on the roof?
qa.a: His aunt Lakshmi found him there.

qa.q: How does Farhan's handling of trouble at sixteen differ from his handling at twenty?
qa.a: At sixteen one setback and a family quarrel were handled with a list of retakes and a talk with his teacher, with an aunt's support. At twenty a failed paper, his father's hospital stay and the fee date arrived together, so he went to the counsellor and the scholarship office and the adviser for help.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he stopped answering messages and slept badly?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and worn down, carrying several pressures at once.

qa.q: What could Farhan do to keep going as the term continues?
qa.a: He could keep in touch with Ramesh, tell the faculty adviser about the paper, and ask a friend or relative to help with hospital visits so he is not carrying it alone.

grounding: The same person copes with adversity at sixteen with a family crisis and bad results, and at twenty with a failed paper, hospital stay and fees, by seeking help.

passage: At ten, Siddharth's cousin Kamal announced at lunch that he had seen a dog drive a car. Siddharth put his spoon down. "I think you're joking," he said. "Dogs can't reach the pedals." Kamal grinned and admitted it was a film. Siddharth did not call him a liar; he had wanted to check the story, and it turned out to be a good one. At twenty-five, Siddharth was at his desk when a message pinged: "You have won a prize! Pay a small fee within ten minutes to claim it." His colleague Pranav leaned over, curious. "Maybe it's real?" Siddharth read the sender's number twice. "The urgency is odd. I never entered anything." He opened the company's own website, found no such prize, and reported the message to the phone company. Pranav laughed. "You believe nothing." Siddharth shook his head. "I believe plenty. I just check first." That evening he happily accepted a friend's news of a promotion without one question.

qa.q: What did Kamal say he had seen at lunch?
qa.a: He said he had seen a dog drive a car.

qa.q: How is Siddharth's doubt at ten like his doubt at twenty-five?
qa.a: At ten he said he thought Kamal was joking because dogs cannot reach the pedals, and at twenty-five he doubted the urgent prize message and checked the company's own site. Both times he checked the facts and did not decide the person was bad.

qa.q: What was Siddharth thinking when he read the prize message twice?
qa.a: He was wary and suspicious, noting the urgency and that he never entered anything.

qa.q: What could Pranav do the next time a surprising offer arrives?
qa.a: Pranav could pause, check the sender's number and the company's own website, and ask Siddharth before paying anything.

grounding: The same person uses doubt to check things at ten and twenty-five: questioning a tall story with humour, and verifying an urgent prize message before acting.

passage: At two, Maria stood in the doorway and curled her finger at her father Gautam, beckoning him toward the sofa. "Come." When he came, she gave him a thumbs-up with her whole fist and laughed. She had copied both from him and had no idea what they meant; she only knew that people smiled back. At nine, at her grandmother Farida's house, Maria bent to touch her Nani's feet as the visitors did, and Farida rested a warm hand on her head. Later a relative she barely knew reached out, waiting for the same. Maria stiffened and stepped behind her father. Gautam said lightly, "Maria may fold her hands and say namaste instead." No one made a fuss. Maria let out her breath. At twenty-four, she stood in a queue at the post office and the clerk stayed late to find her missing parcel. Maria placed her hand over her heart. "Thank you. Truly. You've saved me a long trip." The clerk smiled. Her warm voice and steady eyes did as much as her hand.

qa.q: Whose feet did Maria touch at her grandmother's house?
qa.a: She touched her Nani's feet.

qa.q: How does Maria's use of gestures change between two, nine and twenty-four?
qa.a: At two she copied a beckoning finger and thumbs-up without understanding them, at nine she touched her Nani's feet to show respect but was allowed to fold her hands with the uneasy relative, and at twenty-four she put a hand over her heart to thank the clerk. Over the years the gestures gained meaning and choice.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when the unfamiliar relative waited for her to touch feet?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and unsure, so she stiffened and stepped behind her father.

qa.q: What could Gautam do to help Maria show respect in ways that suit her?
qa.a: He can teach her other ways to greet elders, like folding her hands, and make clear she is never forced to touch anyone.

grounding: One person's conventional gestures across ages: copied beckoning and thumbs-up at two, touching an elder's feet with choice at nine, and hand over heart to thank someone at twenty-four.

passage: At nine, Sachin had been taught at home that looking an elder straight in the eye was rude, so when his teacher Vishal spoke to him, he kept his eyes on his shoes. "Look at me when I'm talking," Vishal said, and Sachin's stomach dropped. He lifted his eyes for a second and then dropped them again. That evening his mother explained that at school looking at the speaker means listening, while at home lowering the eyes shows respect. The next day Sachin told Vishal, "At home we look down to be polite," and Vishal nodded and said he understood. At twenty, Sachin spent a summer in an office abroad. While talking to a colleague, Swati, he stood close, the way he did with friends back home. She took a step back, then another. He felt a hot flush of rejection and thought she disliked him. Days later, another intern explained that people there like more space. Sachin tried standing an arm's length away. Swati's shoulders eased and the conversations grew easy and friendly.

qa.q: What did Sachin look at when his teacher spoke to him?
qa.a: He kept his eyes on his shoes.

qa.q: How does Sachin's experience with eye contact at nine relate to standing close at twenty?
qa.a: At nine, looking down showed respect at home but looked like not listening at school, and at twenty standing close felt friendly to him but made Swati step back. In both cases the same behaviour had a different meaning in another place, and understanding the other's habit helped.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when Swati stepped back?
qa.a: He felt rejected and hurt, believing she disliked him.

qa.q: What could Sachin do next time he moves to a place with new habits?
qa.a: He could watch how others stand and look, ask a friendly colleague what is usual, and adjust.

grounding: The same person meets opposite meanings for the same behaviour: eye contact at nine and personal space at twenty, and learns to translate between habits.

passage: In class, nine-year-old Ankita felt a giggle rising when the boy in front dropped his eraser. She pressed her lips together, stared at her page, and held it in, shoulders shaking, until the bell rang. Then she ran to the playground and laughed until she had to hold her sides. At fifteen, Ankita's best friend stopped talking to her, and she kept her face blank in the corridor so no one could see. At home she said "Fine" to everything. Her older cousin Tarun noticed her plate untouched and said, "I'm going for a walk. Want to come? We don't have to talk." Halfway round the block she began to speak. At twenty, Ankita sat before Imran, the interview panel's chair, keeping her hands folded, her voice level and her reactions small. When a question surprised her, she did not blink. The interview went well. Afterwards, on the steps outside, she leaned against the wall and let out a long breath, tired from being so careful.

qa.q: What did the boy in front of Ankita drop in class?
qa.a: He dropped his eraser.

qa.q: How does Ankita's restraint show up at nine, fifteen and twenty, and what does each cost her?
qa.a: At nine she held in a giggle until the bell and then laughed on the playground, at fifteen she kept a blank face and said "Fine" to hide her hurt, and at twenty she kept her reactions small in the interview and felt tired afterwards. Restraint was useful, but it needed a place to be released or shared.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she said "Fine" to everything at home?
qa.a: She felt hurt and sad about losing her best friend, and she was hiding it from everyone.

qa.q: How could Tarun keep helping Ankita when she is holding things in?
qa.a: Tarun can keep offering low-pressure chances to talk, like a walk, and let Ankita begin in her own time.

grounding: The same person practises restraint at three ages: holding in a giggle at nine, a blank face at fifteen and a muted manner in an interview at twenty, each with a cost or release.

passage: At two, twins Shalini and Afreen played very differently. Shalini scaled the sofa arm, then the table, shrieking with joy, and their mother Preeti stayed within arm's reach and moved the vase. Afreen stood at the edge of the rug, holding her mother's dupatta, watching the new wooden toy for a long time before she touched it, and then only with one finger. Preeti let her take her time. At fifteen, Shalini's friends dared her to cross the railway line as a shortcut and she felt the thrill of them watching. Before the outing Preeti had said, "If you ever want out, text me the word 'mango' and I will call you home, no questions." Shalini sent the word. Preeti phoned and asked her to come home for something important. Later Shalini admitted she'd been scared. At twenty, Afreen was offered a place on a summer project in another city. She read about it many times, asked three people and made a list of everything that could go wrong. The deadline passed. She stayed home, safe, and afterwards watched the others' photos.

qa.q: What was the word Shalini could text to her mother?
qa.a: She could text her mother the word "mango."

qa.q: How do the sisters' different temperaments show at two, fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: At two Shalini climbed while Afreen watched and touched with one finger, at fifteen Shalini took a dare with friends watching until she sent her mother the word, and at twenty Afreen checked everything and let the deadline pass. Boldness needed a safe way out, and caution might miss a chance.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she sent the word to her mother?
qa.a: She felt scared and wanted to leave the dare, but didn't want to lose face in front of her friends.

qa.q: What small step could help Afreen try something new without feeling reckless?
qa.a: She could pick one small trial, like a short visit to the city or a call with past participants, so fear does not decide everything.

grounding: One family shows risk tolerance across years: a bold and a cautious toddler, a teenager taking risks with friends watching, and a cautious young adult who passes on a chance.
